detail.abstract: This paper develops an overlapping generations model of a general purpose technology transition and uses cohort welfare accounting to study how general purpose technologies redistribute welfare across ages, occupations, and wealth positions. In the benchmark, the largest losses fall on workers in substitution exposed occupations who are in the middle of the working life because codification erodes incumbent human capital while scalable technology assets are revalued upward. Fixed replacement and matched ordinary product cycle counterfactuals indicate that faster replacement is not the main source of incidence. Instead, the contrast with an ordinary product cycle reflects the joint contribution of codification, residual task reallocation, higher technology capability, frontier productivity, and asset revaluation. Richer environments with within cohort heterogeneity, borrowing constraints, retraining, and occupation switching preserve the same policy ranking: retraining subsidies materially reduce losses, whereas rent sharing and replacement wedges do little. The key policy margin in general purpose technology transitions is repairing the human wealth held by workers.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the causal effect of major hurricanes on alcohol purchasing behavior. Natural disasters influence health behaviors through both economic and psychological channels, yet objective evidence on these responses remains limited. We combine NielsenIQ retail scanner data with NOAA hurricane tracks for nine major hurricanes in the southern United States between 2008 and 2019. To identify dynamic treatment effects, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences framework. Our results show a significant 10.6% increase in alcohol sales during the event week, reflecting pre landfall stockpiling. This behavior is most pronounced in "open" states with weaker supply regulations and for alcohol products. Following landfall, alcohol sales decline sharply by 18.4% and 8.4% in the subsequent two weeks. This suppression persists for up to twelve weeks in rural areas and for liquor products. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that post hurricane declines are driven primarily by food stores and, separately, rural counties. These patterns suggest that negative income effects and persistent financial stress outweigh psychological triggers that might otherwise increase consumption. By using high-frequency transaction data, we overcome the limitations of self-reported surveys and provide systematic evidence on how extreme weather shocks affect risky health behaviors. Our findings underscore the importance of targeting disaster recovery policies toward vulnerable populations to mitigate the long-term economic and health consequences of natural disasters.

detail.abstract:
In June 2024, the founder of New Zealand Native Oils (NZ Oils) was facing the critical decision of whether to take her business international or remain domestic. She established NZ Oils six years earlier to produce and market skin care products made of organic extracts from manuka and other native plants in New Zealand. The start-up had grown rapidly since its inception within the domestic market, especially during the COVID-19 period, when demand for antibacterial skin-care products skyrocketed. With the reopening of national borders worldwide and the bouncing back of international logistics after the global pandemic, the founder was increasingly drawn to consider the decision of whether to pursue the international market. This case is intended for an undergraduate or graduate-level class that aims to teach about the internationalization decision, especially in the start-up context. By focusing on the decision of whether to take a business international, the case is particularly suitable for an early session of a course that will subsequently cover such topics as patterns, stages, modes, pace, and timing of the internationalization process. While the case can be approached from multiple angles, the topics of international entrepreneurship, international business, and strategic management are especially recommended.

The case provides comprehensive details concerning the entrepreneur, the start-up, the national context, and the venture’s preliminary international experiences. Through reading the case and working on the assigned questions, students have the opportunity to do the following: Learn the internationalization motives of firms. Understand the unique advantages and challenges for start-ups of going international. Explore the role of the individual entrepreneur in the internationalization decision. Delineate success factors for the international expansion of start-ups.

detail.abstract:
Trust has been described as “perhaps the single most powerful relationship marketing tool available to a company” (Berry, 1995, p. 242). When one party trusts the other, he or she is willing to risk dependence on the other to obtain a goal. Consequently, trust is a critical influence in the development of business-to-business (B2B) relationships and relationship commitment. Trust is a fundamental construct in relational exchange because relationships characterised by trust are so highly valued that parties will desire to commit themselves to such relationships. Trust is also one of the factors that differentiate relationships from mere transactions (Hess & Story, 2005) and enjoys wide acceptance among scholars as a key facilitator of interorganisational relationship development; however, the  construct has not been widely explored within the context of service failure. Undeniably, trust is a central tenet of relationship marketing and a useful construct for measuring the likelihood of customer loyalty as well as for predicting future purchase frequency.

Many studies have considered how trust develops, but there is limited research specifically investigating how trust might be recovered after it has been harmed in the context of B2B relationships. Scholars note that previous research on business relationships and trust have been largely static, cross-sectional and variable-focused correlational explanations of trust (Huang & Wilkinson, 2013). This shortcoming of current research is that it does not show how different variables change and develop, interrelatedly, and what types of relations
emerge, in terms of different mixes and values of variables, under different conditions,(Wong, Wilkinson, & Young, 2010).

To address this shortcoming, this research features two studies specifically examining trust recovery in B2B relationships following service failure and a breach of trust from the perspective of the buying organisation. Study One presents an exploration of the  determinants of trust recovery following service failure through qualitative enquiry and thematic analysis. This analysis reveals eight factors that contribute to trust recovery following service failure of both a cognitive- and affective-dominant nature. Both cognitiveand affective-dominant perceptions are essential causal conditions when seeking to understand buyers’ estimations of trust in a B2B relationship (Franklin & Marshall, 2019) and may be combined in different configurations in order to achieve trust recovery. However, limited research has incorporated these factors to the configurational analysis of high levels of trust recovery success following service failure in a B2B context. 

Toward this end, Study Two adopts a configurational approach through qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) to investigate the interrelatedness between both causal and contextual conditions when seeking to recover trust with a buying organisation. This analysis unravels configurations of these causal and contextual conditions, offering theoretical consensus surrounding the role of key constituents of interorganisational trust recovery, and their interrelatedness, in a B2B context. Additionally, this research offers managers guidance regarding different ways to achieve successful trust recovery with their buying organisations. Presenting managers with a variety of optional choices in the design and deployment of reparative solutions invites an economy, or efficiency, in their efforts by choosing the configuration that best fits with the supplying organisation’s strategy, culture or already existing resource availability.

detail.abstract: Customer Trust Infrastructure (CTI) is a founded discipline concerned with the organizational design conditions under which trust between brands and customers forms, persists, and recovers from disruption. Since its formal establishment in March 2026, the CTI has introduced several original theoretical constructs that together constitute a vocabulary for diagnosing, designing, and repairing customer trust at both the individual and systemic levels. This paper serves as a formal definitional record for three core constructs: the Customer Trust Equation, Customer Anomie, and Parasocial Trust Transfer. Each construct is defined, situated within its theoretical lineage, and positioned within the broader CTI framework. This is a conceptual vocabulary paper, and its purpose is definitional and archival rather than empirical. The empirical validation of these constructs is an active agenda within CTI's research program. Researchers working in consumer behavior, organizational trust, and market sociology are invited to engage with, build on, and critique this vocabulary.

detail.abstract:
Bangladesh stands at a vital and sensitive juncture in its structural transformation - a period in which the domestic retention and quality of human capital will determine whether the economy can move beyond factor-driven growth toward productivity-led development. This paper investigates the formation of migration intentions among college and university students, and offers an early-stage lens on the mechanisms through which human capital is diverted before it enters the productive economy. By shifting analytical focus from employed professionals to student populations, the study captures a pre-labour market stage that conventional brain drain models overlook. This stage is arguably the most consequential phase for long-run human capital development. Drawing on endogenous growth theory, which positions human capital as the engine of sustained productivity through knowledge spillovers and innovation diffusion, this paper shows how pre-labour market emigration represents a particularly costly form of talent loss that forecloses even initial domestic contributions before they begin.  
The paper applies a push-pull migration framework and integrates it with the Theory of Planned Behavior, extending traditional models to incorporate student-specific push factors including perceived education system quality gaps, higher study opportunity constraints, graduate job market risk, political instability and peer migration norms. These factors collectively capture the mismatch between domestic human capital formation conditions and international alternatives that shape migration intentions before individuals enter the professional labour market. We have used a quantitative cross-sectional survey of 286 students across public and private institutions. The study employs multivariate OLS regression to identify the structural drivers of migration intent and Ordered Logit estimation as a robustness check. Our OLS model achieves joint statistical significance (F = 21.05, p < 0.001) and explains 45.8% of the variation in migration intention (R² = 0.458). Findings show three variables as significant predictors. They are improved lifestyle abroad (β = 0.272, β* = 0.284, p < 0.001), graduate job market risk (β = 0.188, β* = 0.235, p < 0.001) and education system quality gap (β = 0.136, β* = 0.148, p = 0.020). Through the ordered logit robustness check, we confirm that lifestyle abroad and graduate job market risk remain highly significant across functional forms, while the education quality gap result is directionally consistent but moderately sensitive to model specification. Students enrolled at public institutions exhibit significantly lower migration intentions than their private institution counterparts (β = −0.304, p = 0.021) which reflects differential career orientation and domestic opportunity structures across Bangladesh's tertiary education landscape. The findings indicate that migration intentions are primarily driven by perceived deficiencies in the domestic human capital development environment which are inferior educational quality, weak graduate labour market returns and a wide human development gap relative to destination countries. The intentions are less driven by political instability or social pressure alone. The policy implications are clear and substantial. Student phase migration intentions represent an early-stage diversion of Bangladesh's human capital pipeline, with significant downstream consequences for labour market composition and the economy's structural transformation trajectory. Effective and convincing human capital retention policy must intervene before entry into the labour market. Policymakers must target educational quality gaps and career expectation differentials that drive pre-professional migration decisions. We receive empirically grounded guidance from this study for early policy intervention, education reform, and human capital retention strategy in Bangladesh.

detail.title: Sticky Narratives: How Micro-Influencers Engage and Retain Their Audience Through Storytelling
detail.abstract: This research examines the vital role of storytelling in modern marketing communications and interactions, focusing on micro influencers on social media platforms like Instagram. This work aims to evaluate the effectiveness of storytelling strategies employed by influencers in engaging and retaining audiences. This qualitative analysis identifies four key narrative strategies: educating, evaluating, advising and entertaining. These strategies are assessed for their impact on audience engagement and 'stickiness'. The findings reveal that each narrative strategy uniquely affects audience interaction and engagement on social media. The study underscores the significance of micro influencers in shaping brand engagement, emphasising the need for a balance between creative freedom and brand alignment. Importantly, it highlights how influencers leverage personal narratives to build trust and authenticity with their audience, thus enhancing brand image and audience connection. This trend towards authenticity and personal narratives in digital communication reflects a broader societal shift where consumers value transparency and genuine connection. This research also calls for further exploration of diverse narrative strategies across different domains and the role of technology in empowering influencers. This study contributes to understanding digital influencer storytelling and its impact on brand image and audience engagement, offering new perspectives on influencer marketing strategies in the digital era. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1177/14413582251340442

detail.abstract: This study investigates how vulnerable populations achieve empowered digital safety through distinct combinations of personal, social, and institutional conditions. Drawing on survey data from 575 respondents across six vulnerable groups in Australasia, we applied fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) within a Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) framework. The results reveal multiple equifinal pathways to empowerment, highlighting the consistent role of stakeholder support and personal digital safety practices. However, subgroup analyses demonstrate important variations that cultural influence was decisive for Indigenous users, while NGO and educational support were central for rural and elderly participants. Awareness and compliance emerged as broadly core but not sufficient alone, and family support was consistently peripheral. The findings advance theory by reframing empowerment as a systemic capability and inform practice by underscoring the need for contextually tailored interventions.

detail.abstract: This article develops the second stage of the algorithmic colonialism framework. The first paper, Algorithmic Colonialism: The Dawn of a New Era of Colonialism, argued that colonial power has not disappeared but has been reconfigured through digital, behavioural, cognitive, and algorithmic forms of control. This second paper advances the framework by distinguishing data colonialism from algorithmic colonialism. Data colonialism explains the extraction of human life as data. Algorithmic colonialism explains what can happen after extraction: the conversion of data into systems of prediction, behavioural steering, social classification, epistemic filtering, dependency, and identity capture. The central argument is that the contemporary colonial frontier is not only land, labour, or raw materials, but increasingly the behavioural and identity structure of the human being. Artificial intelligence, platform infrastructures, recommendation systems, predictive analytics, biometric technologies, automated governance, and digital dependency do not merely observe society. Under conditions of unequal power, they may participate in organising attention, shaping preference, ranking visibility, directing behaviour, and mediating the conditions through which individuals and communities understand themselves. The paper builds on debates around digital colonialism, data colonialism, surveillance capitalism, the colonial matrix of AI power, Indigenous data sovereignty, linguistic marginalisation, and global AI governance. It extends these debates through the IAAP framework, Identity in the Age of Algorithmic Power, which analyses identity capture across four domains: memory, emotion, choice, and behaviour. The paper argues that decolonising AI requires more than data protection, ethical principles, or technological inclusion. It also requires protection of human agency, cultural memory, epistemic autonomy, behavioural freedom, and the capacity of societies to shape their own digital futures.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework for evaluating the effects of information sharing and applies it to the Agri Stats information exchange among turkey processors. In the year after the exchange abruptly ended, the retail price of participating processors fell by 5.1% relative to other processors. Descriptive evidence suggests both conduct and information effects played a role. I build a structural model to isolate the two, letting me test for changes in conduct while accounting for how sharing affects firms' information sets. I reject the hypothesis of zero conduct effect, and estimate that Agri Stats clients acted like they internalized 47% of their competitors' profits while sharing information. Not accounting for information effects leads to underestimation of conduct effects. Preliminary counterfactual simulations suggest that information effects by themselves are procompetitive and reduce profits in aggregate, potentially supporting an inference of collusion from information sharing.

title: Harness Alignment and Harness Drift: Why Intent, Unlike Correctness, Resists Automation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
By early 2026, the discourse around agent harnesses — the configuration layer of skills, rules, prompts, and documentation shaping an LLM agent's behavior — has named two activities: harness engineering, the reactive practice of ensuring an agent never repeats a mistake, and harness optimization, autonomous search over harness code for benchmark score. Both run against fixed, checkable criteria. The activity on the other side — keeping the harness aligned with what its operator now wants, where the criterion moves — is performed daily and has, to the author's knowledge, no established name.

The paper defines harness alignment — the continuous, human-gated activity of keeping an agent's harness aligned with the operator's evolving intent — and its failure mode, harness drift. The three defining properties — continuous, human-gated, bidirectional — follow from a single root: intent, unlike correctness, cannot be automated the same way — it has no verifier outside the operator, and moves as the operator's judgment sharpens; verifying intent sharpens the judgment doing it, so the loop moves its own target. An automated check freezes intent into a specification, reducing its automatable part to correctness work. A four-domain search found no established term covering all three; an audit shows 2026 drift coinages severed from the classical lineage that harness drift bridges. A six-phase cycle (Research, Extract, Curate, Promote, Measure, Maintain) operationalizes it over a memory structure whose boundary separates freely-writable records from gated behavior-shaping artifacts.

Failure has two layers: artifact-side harness drift, and a human-side twin — gate complacency, deskilling, delegation-feedback divergence — anchored in the automation-complacency and ironies-of-automation literatures — structural inference, not measurement. Two running instances, differing in substrate, model, and knowledge genre, are offered as portability evidence, not efficacy. All of it comes from months-old practice — provisional judgments offered for testing, not settled practice.

detail.abstract: India's data centre sector is expanding at a pace with no historical parallel. From a base of approximately 190 operational facilities in 2026, the country is set to add 87 more sites across 17 states, with total installed power projected to reach 8 GW by 2030-a fivefold increase from the 2025 installed base of approximately 1.5 GW. Yet the cities absorbing this growth-Chennai, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Delhi-NCR-are among the most water-stressed in the world. India's data centres consumed roughly 150 billion litres of freshwater in 2025; that figure is on course to more than double to 358 billion litres by 2030. Unlike most industrialised nations, India is building the majority of its next generation of facilities before any mandatory sustainability standards exist: only five of India's fifteen state data centre policies contain any environmental parameter whatsoever. This paper argues that the only effective strategy is to mandate sustainable design for all new construction before the next wave is built because retrofitting existing facilities is technically disruptive and economically prohibitive. Drawing on engineering data, investigative reporting, and international precedent, the paper proposes specific, measurable standards covering water usage effectiveness (WUE), cooling technology thresholds, energy sourcing, and hardware lifecycle management-including the novel and unaddressed challenge of dielectric fluid waste from liquid-cooled systems. The paper also maps the 87 upcoming facilities against India's water-stress zones and identifies which state policies require urgent strengthening.

title: Advantages of ERP Systems based on Microservice Architectures for their Users

detail.title: Advantages of ERP Systems based on Microservice Architectures for their Users
detail.abstract:
Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems have traditionally been implemented as monolithic applications. While this architectural style offers simplicity and strong data consistency, it increasingly struggles to meet the scalability, flexibility, and maintainability requirements of modern organisations. Microservice architectures provide an alternative approach by decomposing ERP functionality into independently deployable services. However, organisations often lack structured guidance for assessing whether the advantages of microservice-based ERP systems justify the additional operational complexity they introduce. This paper systematically investigates the advantages of ERP systems based on microservice architectures for their users and translates the findings into a four-layer reference model. Using reference modelling as the research methodology, the model traces a causal chain from fundamental microservice properties through technical effects to user-facing advantages and architectural recommendations. The analysis draws on a comparison of monolithic and microservice architectures, ERP process case studies, and a review of relevant literature on architectural trade-offs and decision criteria. 
The resulting model identifies five key user advantages: higher availability, better performance under load, faster feature delivery, lower vendor lock-in, and flexible integration. A scenario-based decision framework maps these advantages to organisational contexts and stakeholder groups, supported by an illustrative application example. Migration strategies, particularly the Strangler Fig pattern, are discussed as practical approaches for transitioning from monolithic to microservice-based architectures. The paper contributes a reusable, decision-oriented reference model that supports organisations in evaluating the suitability of microservice architectures in ERP environments while recognising the operational challenges and contextual factors that influence their successful adoption.

title: The Money Function: An Information Theory of Money

detail.title: The Money Function: An Information Theory of Money

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts to declare
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: This paper assembles a value theory of money from two formalisms not previously joined: Keynes's logical theory of probability and Shannon's mathematical theory of communication. Money is defined as the unfulfilled portion of a forward contract, created in full at signing and destroyed payment by payment. The value of such a contract is a conditional probability of fulfillment, V(C) = Σₖ sₖ•π(k|h), with π < 1 always, because no information from the future exists. Payment is the resolution of uncertainty in Shannon's exact sense; law functions as money's errorcorrecting code; and interest prices the residual uncertainty no contract can eliminate. Keynes's "weight of the argument" enters as a second state variable whose collapse, not whose level, locates crises. Three dynamic results follow: monetary continuity is an unguaranteed flow condition; debt deflation is an information cascade; and the state space is endogenous, so equilibrium concepts do not apply. Sovereign money does not escape uncertainty but relocates it: a conservation law.

detail.abstract: Illinois state expenditures for fiscal year 2025 (July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025). Illinois ended FY2025 with expenditures of $119.51 billion and revenues of $118.16 billion, a near-balanced result despite a nominal fiscal gap of $1.35 billion. Both figures reflect the steady upward trend in state finances since 1998, punctuated only by the FY2022 surge in federal COVID-19 relief funding (Figure 1). Medicaid remains Illinois’ largest expenditure category, growing 7.48% to $35.94 billion in FY2025—outpacing its already-rapid 27-year compound annual growth rate of 7.27%. Several other categories have also expanded significantly, including transportation (+13.38%), Human Services (+7.53%), and State Employee Healthcare (+20.62%). The healthcare surge—rising from $3.16 billion to $3.81 billion—may be partly attributable to a mandated expansion of the State Employees’ Group Insurance Program (SEGIP) requiring coverage of injectable medications for adults with prediabetes, gestational diabetes, or obesity. Medical care inflation in the Chicago area was only 2.5% and SEGIP enrollment grew by a modest 4.8% (17,258 participants) during the same period. The FY2025 fiscal gap, while negative, is less concerning than it may appear. Based on this analysis, Illinois’ FY2025 spending and revenue were approximately balanced after accounting for the spenddown of Covid-era funds and the transfer of excess funds from the income tax refund fund. Going forward, Medicaid’s long-term trajectory, slow growth in sales tax revenues, and federal funding uncertainty represent the most significant fiscal risks to monitor.

detail.abstract: Green bonds have become a key instrument for financing projects with environmental and climate-related benefits, amid the rapid growth of ESG investments across institutional, wealth, and retail investors. While the global green bond market has expanded substantially across both developed and emerging economies, evidence on how equity investors respond to green bond issuances in Asian markets remains limited. This paper examines stock market reactions to green bond announcements by publicly listed firms in Asia over the period 2014-2025. It combines a descriptive overview of green bond market development across major Asian economies with an event-study analysis based on the market model, used to estimate cumulative abnormal returns around announcement dates. The empirical analysis considers heterogeneity across countries, sectors, first-time and repeated issuances, developed and developing markets, sub-periods, and the pre-and post-COVID periods. The results show no statistically significant aggregate stock market reaction across alternative event windows. However, responses vary across countries and sectors, suggesting that equity investors may assess green bond announcements differently depending on the institutional context and the credibility or materiality of the underlying environmental commitment. Overall, the findings indicate that, in Asian equity markets, green bond issuance is generally perceived as a neutral financing decision rather than a systematic short-term value-creating event. The paper contributes by documenting the evolution of Asian green bond markets and by providing baseline empirical evidence on the equity-market implications of green bond announcements in the region.

detail.abstract: The practice of “strategic litigation” has become a settled feature of English judicial review but there has been little attempt so far to take stock of the current state of research into this practice. The following article aims to act as an opener to the nature of strategic litigation in English judicial review. It outlines the key features of this litigation model and evaluates the major trends in the literature. It notes that while the existing research provides important insights into aspects of strategic litigation, there is a need for more specified and comprehensive studies into this practice. In an era where judicial review has come under pointed attack within government, deeper qualitative research into strategic litigation - a practice that is arguably a major cause of the ongoing political backlash against the courts - is essential to provide a clearer understanding as to the legitimacy of this litigation model and the extent to which it can produce the impact desired by its protagonists.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the Employee Ownership Trust (EOT) model, comparing it with traditional partnerships and employee ownership structures like the US Employee Stock Ownership Plans (ESOPs) and the European Coop -ESOPs. It primarily focuses on the crucial distinction of EOTs lacking individual capital accounts for employees due to common ownership and leading to what is termed a "horizon problem" where employees do not recoup their share of retained earnings. The "naked in, naked out" rationale, often used to justify this lack of individual accounts in EOTs, is easily refuted by noting that even professional partnerships described as "naked out" still pay off the partner capital accounts of exiting partners. Furthermore, the "firstcohort problem" is analyzed highlighting how initial employees in an EOT may effectively subsidize the acquisition debt without a mechanism to access their accumulated equity, potentially pressuring a future sale of the firm. Finally, EOTs are distinguished from democratic employee ownership since they have a form of trustee-ownership, where governance ultimately rests with a trust rather than with the employee-beneficiaries.

detail.abstract: This study examines the levels of trust and commitment among members of Gum Arabic Producers Associations (GAPAs) in the Central Gum Arabic Belt of Sudan. Primary data were collected through a social survey of 14 GAPAs, with 338 respondents randomly selected. Additional evidence was gathered from group discussions, in-depth interviews, field observations, and key informants' interviews. The findings indicate that trust is a key driver of member participation and long-term engagement in GAPAs, with important implications for their sustainability. However, trust and commitment are undermined by weak governance, poor communication, and limited member involvement, which often lead to exclusion from decision-making and low participation. In such contexts, members tend to rely on informal or kinship-based forms of trust; participation in leadership roles remains limited; and women's involvement is constrained by cultural barriers. Financial sustainability represents an additional major challenge, as most GAPAs rely heavily on external funding and lack welldefined mechanisms and incentives for member-based capital contributions.

detail.abstract: The 57th annual conference of the UK Society for Co-operative Studies was held on 8-9 May 2026 in Birmingham, hosted by Birmingham Business School at the University of Birmingham. Under the broad theme “Fostering Dialogue, Shared Learning, and Collaboration around the Future of Cooperation”, the conference brought together scholars, practitioners, cooperative developers, policy actors, and members of cooperative organisations at a moment of renewed political attention. The timing was significant. The 2025 International Year of Cooperatives had strengthened the visibility of cooperatives, while in the UK the Labour government’s commitment to double the size of the cooperative and mutual economy by 2035 provided a concrete political horizon. Yet the conference repeatedly showed that recognition does not automatically become institutional capacity. Participants returned to a common set of questions: what kind of growth should the movement pursue, which infrastructures are required to sustain it, and how can cooperation become visible to those who may benefit from it? Rather than reproducing the programme chronologically, this conference letter reconstructs the principal tensions that emerged across the two days: the gap between political ambition and institutional fragility; democracy as a practice rather than a structure; education and visibility as conditions for renewal; the tension between identity and flexibility; and the need to understand cooperative growth ecologically, as the development of a diverse organisational landscape rather than the expansion of a few large organisations.

detail.title: Institutional access and Bitcoin volatility dynamics: evidence from the introduction of a spot Bitcoin ETF (IBIT)
detail.abstract: This study examines whether the launch of the iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) is associated with a persistent reconfiguration of Bitcoin's second-moment dynamics, extending beyond the short-run announcement effects documented in prior event studies. Using a multi-method empirical framework on daily data from 2020 to 2026 and a sustained twenty-eight-month post-event window, we document a durable transformation of volatility, persistence, and tail risk rather than a transitory announcement response. While Chow, HAC-Wald, Andrews sup-F, and PELT procedures fail to reject mean stability, annualized volatility declines by approximately 19% to 28% across estimators, with close-to-close, Parkinson, and Garman-Klass measures all yielding statistically significant reductions. EGARCH(1,1,1) estimates indicate that the implied half-life of volatility shocks shortens from approximately 45 to 12 trading days, with a complementary GJR-GARCH specification yielding a post-IBIT half-life of approximately 25 days; both specifications point to a substantial acceleration of shock dissipation. Extreme downside exposure, measured by 1% Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall, compresses by approximately 44%, with bootstrap inference confirming statistical significance. At the portfolio level, Bitcoin's marginal contribution to tail risk declines by approximately three-quarters at standard allocation weights. Non-parametric ICSS variance-break detection identifies no discrete break within thirty days of the launch, consistent with a gradual regime adjustment rather than an instantaneous structural switch. Robustness tests using weekly returns, exclusion of the April 2024 halving window, and alternative breakpoints confirm the findings. The results contribute to the literature on cryptocurrency risk dynamics by documenting a coincident compression in Bitcoin's second-moment characteristics around the spot ETF era, a pattern distinct from the volatility responses previously documented for derivative-based products. In contrast to short-window event-study evidence, the compression is shown to persist and to extend into the tail of the return distribution and the portfolio risk budget, dimensions outside the scope of an announcement-window design.

detail.title: FMD-RTDETR: Adaptive Feature Calibration for Bladder Epithelial Cell Detection in Multiplexed Immunofluorescence Images
detail.abstract: The accurate detection and quantification of bladder epithelial cell markers is essential for elucidating cell population dynamics and disease progression, yet conventional manual profiling methods remain labor-intensive and highly susceptible to subjective bias. To address the challenges of target localization and dense cell adhesion in complex multiplexed fluorescence backgrounds, we propose the Fluorescent Microcell Detection Real-Time Detection Transformer (FMD-RTDETR), an end-toend object detection framework based on RT-DETR, featuring a novel Adaptive Calibration Feature Fusion (ACFF) module. This module replaces conventional fusion with an Attention-based Fusion Module (AFM) incorporating parameter-free High-Resolution Feature Perception (HRFP) to suppress noise while preserving morphological detail. Additionally, the proposed ACFF integrates Contextual and Spatial Feature Calibration (CFC/SFC) to mitigate semantic dilution and spatial misalignmentduring cross-scale fusion. Evaluated on our custom multi-channel Fluorescent Staining of Bladder Epithelial Cells (FSBEC) dataset, FMD-RTDETR achieves an mAP0.5 of 0.895, outperforming stateof-the-art models in robust bounding box regression, handling cellular adhesion, and multi-class phenotyping across four staining profiles. It also attains 0.901 mAP0.5 on the public DSB2018 dataset, demonstrating strong generalization and enabling precise, high-throughput cell quantification for bladder pathology assessment.

affiliations: and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Operations Area

detail.title: Cloud Value Chains in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative AI is transforming cloud computing from a virtualized service platform into a tightly coupled, capital-intensive value chain spanning upstream supply networks (hardware, energy, and data), midstream AI data centers, and downstream AI platform ecosystems. In this AI era, traditional cloud assumptions-predictable performance from provisioned resources, frictionless elastic scaling, and unconstrained upstream inputs-are breaking down due to heterogeneous training and inference workloads, token-based performance measurement and pricing, and two-sided information asymmetry regarding demand characteristics and providers' hidden operational controls. To address these fundamental changes, this paper proposes an end-to-end framework for analyzing AI-driven cloud value chains from a holistic operations management (OM) perspective. Using this framework, we (i) articulate how AI workloads and production pipelines differ fundamentally from those of traditional cloud computing; (ii) map the key actors and interactions across downstream platform ecosystems, midstream AI data centers, and upstream supply networks; and (iii) synthesize emerging industry practices to develop a research agenda spanning strategic (e.g., coopetition, vertical integration, and long-term capacity expansion under sustainability objectives and policy constraints), tactical (e.g., pricing, capacity reservation and allocation mechanisms, and procurement of hardware, energy, and data services), and operational (e.g., compute pipeline scheduling, congestion control, and grid contingency planning) decisions. The proposed framework helps managers and policymakers diagnose bottlenecks and incentive conflicts while identifying their underlying drivers. In particular, AI platform providers should align pricing and contracting mechanisms with output uncertainty and information asymmetry, while cloud infrastructure and foundation model providers should design capacity reservation, allocation, and real-time pipeline control policies that reflect training-inference differences and throughput-latency tradeoffs. Together, these challenges require coordinated procurement, capacity planning, and operational strategies to scale AI infrastructure efficiently, responsibly, and sustainably.

detail.title: Sovereign Debt, Inflation, and Capital Distortion: Quantifying Argentina’s First-Order Growth Margins
detail.abstract: We assess the medium-run growth potential of Argentina under President Milei’s stabilization-and-reform program by computing alternative scenaro bounds in a calibrated neoclassical framework benchmarked against Latin American, OECD, and post-EU-integration Eastern European peers. Using García-Belenguer et al.  (2026) evidence on the dual sovereign-debt/inflation channel, we treat sovereign-debt cycles and inflation as central macroeconomic forces behind Argentina’s productivity gap relative to regional peers, and Argentina’s high net marginal product of capital as evidence of binding investment-cost distortions. Counterfactual scenario bounds imply medium-term gains in GDP per worker ranging from roughly 11% under a partial-reform lower bound to 65% under a deep-reform upper bound, with a stabilization-oriented intermediate case generating about 24%. Crucially, a solvency-led variant of this intermediate case—in which debt-driven channels are fully resolved while disinflation remains modest—preserves roughly three-quarters of the total gains (about 19% of GDP per worker). This finding demonstrates that restoring fiscal solvency serves as the first-order growth margin at Argentina’s current debt and inflation levels.

detail.abstract: Tropical forests store enormous carbon stocks, yet the global value of keeping them standing accrues to the world while the cost of conservation falls on the countries that own them. Results-based reward funds can close this gap, but tailoring each country's baseline to its own past clearing invites a ratchet effect that blunts incentives. We study the optimal design of a jurisdictional reward fund that pays a common, formula-based reward on net deforestation below a universal reference level, building on the Reversing Deforestation Mechanism of Assunção et al (2025). We first develop a dynamic model and show that static, contemporaneous incentives dominate dynamic, stock-based ones, reducing the design problem to a tractable static screening problem under informational anonymity. We derive closed-form expressions for the optimal reference level, reward rate, and induced emission reductions as functions of the budget, and show that exactly half of any budget is paid out as inframarginal rent. We calibrate the model using data from 76 tropical-forest countries (2002-2024). In a voluntary contributions game, the EU and China form a stable coalition contributing about USD 5.5 billion per year, avoiding 121 MtCO 2 annually.

detail.abstract: We give an exact mechanical interpretation of the cosine Semantic Tube Prediction (STP) loss of Huang et al. (2026) and use it to construct a static architectural diagnostic for the global Lagrangian structure of pretrained transformers. The mathematical core is the closed-form identity  L_STP = 1 − √(1 − |a⊥|² / |d₂|²) , which relates the cosine STP loss between three consecutive hidden states to the magnitude of the component of acceleration normal to the trajectory; we prove the identity algebraically and verify it to machine precision across 1,314 consecutive triplets on GPT-2. Two structural consequences follow immediately: STP loss is blind to the tangential component of acceleration, which we measure to be approximately twice the normal component on GPT-2, and deceleration along the trajectory is the direct mechanical signature of a learned restoring force, with 97.9% of triplets decelerating and a permutation null at z <-11 establishing that sequential token order produces significantly smoother trajectories than random orderings. Both findings replicate on Pythia-160M. These descriptive results establish local hallmarks of damped Lagrangian flow on a bounded attractive potential as a property of trained attention transformers. The natural follow-up-whether the per-layer hidden-state updates globally derive from a single shared scalar potential-is empirically testable. We fit the joint regression Δh_ℓ ≈ α_ℓ · v_ℓ − β_ℓ · ∇V_ψ(h_ℓ) across all layers with a single learned V ψ on frozen checkpoints, and obtain a three-way architectural separator on Tiny Shakespeare: a weight-tied scalar-potential autoregressive flow (used here as a positive control) attains median per-layer test R 2 = 0.957 with a uniform layer profile; a scale-and data-matched 8M-parameter GPT-2-style decoder reaches R 2 = 0.54 with monotonic decay; pretrained GPT-2 small reaches R 2 = 0.46 with a bathtub profile (middle-band mean 0.09). Three independent controls rule out alternative explanations: an oracle fit using the positive control's own potential attains R 2 = 0.931 on the LayerNorm variant (and 1.0000 on the base architecture); a V ψ capacity sweep over a 16× parameter band rules out expressivity limitation; and the separation reproduces under orthogonal token-direction coordinates. All three architectures pass a velocity-aware Jacobian-symmetry test at PCA-16, making local per-step conservativity universal while global shared-potential structure remains architectural. We therefore characterise the Lagrangian content of trained attention transformers as locally conservative but globally not derivable from a shared scalar potential. We provide both a sharper reading of what STP-style training objectives do and do not measure, and a reproducible architectural diagnostic that other globally-Lagrangian designs can be evaluated against.

detail.abstract: We present the Nisa Radial Control Battery (NRCB), a reproducible software workflow for branch-separated control validation of galactic radial-profile diagnostics. The package is designed for astronomical applications in which radial ordering, profile structure, and surrogate comparisons must be kept distinct from physical interpretation. NRCB implements compact, auditable control branches including shuffle/permutation controls, exhaustive circular-shift controls, random-phase surrogate tests, and fixed-reference profile comparisons. The workflow is demonstrated on derived SPARC-based radial-profile products, while raw SPARC data are not redistributed.The release emphasises reproducibility rather than model optimisation. It includes compact derived tables, figure-generation scripts, provenance records, checksum manifests, a preflight validator, and a quickstart notebook that reproduces headline summary values and regenerates manuscript figures without requiring a full production rerun. The software release also separates lightweight paper reproduction from full-production modes that require external data dependencies.NRCB is intended as a controlled computational layer for testing whether apparent radial-profile structure survives appropriate ordering-preserving and phase-randomised controls. The manuscript describes the workflow architecture, implementation safeguards, validation checks, and public release package, providing a reusable basis for transparent control testing in astronomical radial-profile analysis.

detail.abstract:
Background: Accurate non-invasive assessment of liver lesions on multiphasic MRI is essential for diagnostic triage, treatment planning and multidisciplinary management, particularly for distinguishing hepatocellular carcinoma, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, benign lesions and normal liver. Existing AI systems for liver MRI often generate diagnostic outputs without explicitly integrating cross-sequence information or linking predictions to lesion-level visual evidence. This study aimed to develop and evaluate an evidence-linked multimodal MRI-based AI system for liver lesion assessment.

Methods: In this multicentre diagnostic study, multimodal liver MRI data from patients were collected across participating hospitals in China. LiverGrounder was trained using a single-centre cohort and evaluated in independent internal, external, and prospective datasets, including external validation across eight independent centres. The prospective validation study was registered under ChiCTR2600123350. The study included more than 52,000 MRI slices, nearly 30,000 lesion annotations, and more than 188,000 question–answer pairs. LiverGrounder was compared with representative state-of-the-art multimodal vision-language models for lesion localisation, closed-ended diagnostic assessment, open-ended question answering, and report generation. In a prospective reader study, 12 radiologists assessed cases without and with AI assistance. A web-based research interface was implemented to support inspection of multimodal MRI inputs, sequential diagnostic questions, lesion-level visual evidence, model-generated outputs and per-modality gating weights.

Findings: In the internal test set, LiverGrounder achieved an mIoU of 0·5706 for lesion localisation, an average closed-ended diagnostic accuracy of 0·9406, an open-ended F1 score of 0·9585, and report-generation scores of 0·4591 for BLEU-1 and 0·3738 for ROUGE-L. Across eight external validation cohorts, average closed-ended diagnostic accuracies ranged from 0·7135 to 0·8527 and open-ended F1 scores ranged from 0·7561 to 0·8986; in external localisation cohorts, mIoU values ranged from 0·4390 to 0·5218. In the prospective evaluation, LiverGrounder achieved an mIoU of 0·5830, an average closed-ended diagnostic accuracy of 0·8600, an open-ended F1 score of 0·8289, and report-generation scores of 0·3690 for BLEU-1 and 0·2979 for ROUGE-L. Dataset-level improvements over the best-performing baseline model were significant across evaluated tasks (p<0·001). In the prospective reader study, AI assistance improved diagnostic accuracy from 66·0–74·0% to 88·0–96·0% among junior radiologists, reduced average reading time by 40–60% across experience levels, and increased inter-reader agreement from 0·588 to 0·852.

Interpretation: LiverGrounder provides an evidence-linked multimodal MRI-based AI system and research interface for transparent liver lesion assessment. In multicentre and prospective validation, the system improved automated assessment and supported more accurate, spatially grounded and consistent radiologist interpretation, suggesting potential value for non-invasive liver tumour assessment pending further real-world clinical evaluation.

detail.title: Forest Protection and Landslide Regulation: A Global Ecosystem Service Methodology to Value Avoided Human Mortality
detail.abstract: Forests and other natural vegetation can reduce landslide risk by stabilizing slopes, yet their mortality-reduction benefits are rarely quantified at global scale. This study develops a 1 km annual framework that combines the Unified Global Landslide Catalogue with gridded terrain, climate, road, population, and forest-loss data to estimate avoided human mortality from forest-mediated landslide regulation. Landslide occurrence is modeled with a logit specification and conditional fatalities with a hurdle-severity model, then combined under observed and counterfactual deforestation scenarios. The resulting pixel-level estimates are aggregated to countries, World Bank regions, and the globe, and monetized using GDP-adjusted values of a statistical life. Results show that avoided mortality is concentrated in mountain regions of the Andes, Europe, and Asia, while economic values vary with income levels as well as hazard exposure. The framework advances valuation of an underrepresented regulating service by linking hazard modeling with mortality prediction and producing globally comparable, reproducible estimates that can inform natural capital accounting (SEEA) and policy in underrepresented regions.

detail.abstract: This research examines energy efficiency as a crucial tactic for cutting carbon emissions, improving energy security, and bringing down energy expenses in Germany and Norway. Using dynamic panel regression, we examine the various effects of environmental regulations on energy efficiency and find two key findings: (1) at certain levels of stringency, both market-based and command-and-control environmental regulations have a positive impact on total factor energy efficiency, and (2) there are nonlinear relationships between environmental regulations and overall factor energy efficiency. title: Pricing Electricity in Resource-Rich Economies: Reconciling Full-Chain Costs with Macroeconomic Realities

detail.title: Pricing Electricity in Resource-Rich Economies: Reconciling Full-Chain Costs with Macroeconomic Realities
detail.abstract: Traditional electricity pricing models predominantly focus on direct generation and delivery expenses, often neglecting the broader systemic externalities assumed by the public. In monopolistic, heavily subsidized energy markets, this narrow scope obscures the true macroeconomic cost of power generation, systematically transferring unrecovered financial and environmental burdens to public deficits. To address this critical gap, this paper introduces a comprehensive macroeconomic pricing framework that quantifies the total socio-economic cost of electricity. The novel methodology constructs four-tiered pricing benchmarks—ranging from minimal deferred costs to total macroeconomic costs—by aggregating direct operational expenses, hidden resource subsidies, intergenerational scarcity premiums, and systemic damage costs (environmental, health, and value of lost load). Contextualized within Iran’s state-dominated energy market, the model evaluates the magnitude of pricing distortions against these structured tiers using residential consumption data from Mashhad. Rather than merely confirming the existence of subsidies, the empirical findings anatomize the structural deficit, identifying exactly at which tier the current administered tariffs fail to recover operational baselines, thereby mathematically elucidating the paradox of severe electricity shortages in a resource-rich nation. Finally, by integrating a dynamic socioeconomic calibration mechanism that balances cost-reflectivity with consumer affordability, this research provides a rigorous, scalable diagnostic and policy blueprint. This framework is highly applicable to other resource-rich or transitional economies seeking a phased, mathematically grounded pathway out of energy subsidy traps toward sustainable grid management.

detail.abstract: Climate change and increasing urban densification intensify the urban heat island effect, exacerbating thermal stress and associated human health risks. Urban trees mitigate local heat stress through shading and evapotranspiration, thereby supporting well-being in the built environment. However, while the environmental impacts of buildings are monetized, the economic valuation of outdoor thermal comfort remains limited. Within a planning competition context, a heat-related cost–benefit analysis of the outdoor environment under current and future predicted climate conditions was developed, focusing on realistic planning scenarios. Outdoor thermal comfort was quantified using ENVI-met simulations, and heat-related cost savings were estimated based on the proportion of the study area exposed to extreme heat stress. The results indicate that preserving existing trees, including implementing tree protection measures, yields a more favorable cost-benefit analysis (CBA) ratio than removal and replacement over the life cycle. While additional tree planting further improves thermal comfort and reduces heat-related costs, higher life-cycle costs result in only moderate CBA performance. Our study highlights the importance of prioritizing urban tree preservation as a key strategy for climate adaptation and public health protection in early planning decisions.

detail.abstract: Enterprises in regulated industries increasingly rely on AI-assisted decision making, yet deploying large language models (LLMs) at scale introduces persistent tensions between inferential performance, data privacy, and regulatory compliance. This paper proposes the Hybrid Edge-Aware LLM (HEAL) framework, an architecture that combines edge-side anonymisation, federated learning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and cloud-based foundation model inference to address these tensions simultaneously. The design routes sensitive data through a local privacy filter before any remote inference occurs, reducing re-identification risk while preserving the contextual richness needed for high-quality outputs. title: The Asymptote of the Neutral: From Barthes's Degree Zero to the Deconstruction of the Proper -A Poststructuralist Genealogy of Writing beyond Bourgeois Normativity
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Asymptote of the Neutral: From Barthes's Degree Zero to the Deconstruction of the Proper -A Poststructuralist Genealogy of Writing beyond Bourgeois Normativity
detail.abstract:
Introduction: The Triple Aporia of the Neutral

Roland Barthes’s intellectual trajectory, often fragmented by periodisation into an early Marxist-semiological phase, a middle structuralist moment, and a late hedonistic-poststructuralist turn, conceals a deeper, more subterranean continuity: the relentless pursuit of a writing that would escape the threefold appropriation of meaning by bourgeois normativity. This normativity operates through three interlocking mechanisms—naturalisation (the transformation of the historical into the eternal), universalisation (the presentation of class-specific interests as human universals), and proprietarisation (the reduction of textual polysemy to the authorial proper name). Barthes’s response, first articulated in Writing Degree Zero (1953), is the concept of écriture blanche, a “white writing” or “degree zero” that would strip language of its mythological surplus and return it to a state of neutral, pre-signifying transparency. The exemplary literary realisation of this ideal, for the early Barthes, is Albert Camus’s The Stranger (1942), whose paratactic prose, systematic use of the passé composé, and refusal of metaphor appear to constitute a language delivered from the servitude of predestined meaning. Yet Barthes immediately recognised the constitutive aporia of this project: the zero degree, as soon as it is named and recognised, becomes a new positivity, a recognisable style, a commodity recuperated by the very literary institution it sought to negate. “This transparent language, initiated by Camus’s The Stranger,” Barthes writes, “achieves a style of absence which is almost an ideal absence of style; but this absence is immediately caught up in the mechanism of Literature” (Barthes 1968, 77). This failure, however, did not lead Barthes to abandon the zero-degree project; rather, it drove him to relocate its battlefield from the literary text to the writing subject itself. Roland Barthes by Roland Barthes (1975) enacts an autobiographical experiment in which the author’s proper name, the last redoubt of bourgeois proprietarisation, is subjected to the same semiological ascesis previously applied to the classical sentence. The present essay argues that this trajectory—from Camus’s white writing to Barthes’s fragmented autobiography—constitutes a sustained, if paradoxical, struggle against what can be termed the “metaphysics of the proper”: the bourgeois conviction that meaning, property, and selfhood are stable, transparent, and naturally owned. Through a dense dialogue with Jacques Derrida’s critique of presence, Gilles Deleuze’s theory of minor literature and the body without organs, Slavoj Žižek’s Lacanian reading of ideology, Michel Foucault’s analysis of the author-function, Jean-François Lyotard’s concept of the differend, Julia Kristeva’s semiotic chora, and Jean Baudrillard’s orders of simulacra, this essay will demonstrate that the zero degree is not a style to be achieved but an ethical asymptote—a perpetual practice of de-propriation that keeps writing at the limit of the sayable, exposing the ideological closure of every naturalised sign.

This report presents credible, market-supported estimates of annual farmland values and cash rental rates across twelve defined agricultural regions in the northeastern United States, based on verified sales data collected for calendar year 2025. Prepared by the Northeast Chapter of the American Society of Farm Managers and Rural Appraisers (ASFMRA) in collaboration with Cornell University's Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management and Cornell Cooperative Extension, the study covers six regions in New York State (Western New York, Southern Tier, Central New York, Adirondacks, Capital Region, and Hudson Valley), four regions in Vermont (Northwest, Northeast, Southern, and Connecticut River Valley), Southern New England (Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut), and Northwestern Pennsylvania.

For each region, the report documents per-acre value ranges across farmland classes—high-quality cropland, medium-quality cropland, low-quality cropland or pasture, woodland and maple sugarbush, and wasteland or recreational land—along with cash rental rate ranges, activity trends, and qualitative market narratives. Across the twelve regions, land value trends in 2025 were largely stable to modestly increasing compared with 2024, with several regions exhibiting limited transaction volumes that reflect the characteristically low turnover of the Northeast farmland market. Key demand drivers identified include ongoing farm consolidation and operational expansion, competing demand from recreational and lifestyle-oriented buyers, the lasting influence of COVID-19-era rural migration trends, geopolitical uncertainty and input cost pressures, growing agritourism and value-added agricultural sectors, a thriving maple industry in Vermont and the Adirondacks, and the influence of proximity to major metropolitan areas—particularly in the Hudson Valley and Southern New England regions.

The report also highlights region-specific dynamics, including the specialized cranberry market in Massachusetts, declining vineyard values in Erie County, Pennsylvania following processor consolidation, the role of conservation easements in shaping buyer pools, and expanding recreational land demand in the Adirondacks and Northeast Vermont. This publication represents the most geographically comprehensive edition to date and expands prior coverage to include Southern New England and Northwestern Pennsylvania for the first time. Future editions are intended to continue expanding coverage across the broader Northeast.

title: Stablecoins, Digital Dollarization, and Financial Self-determination in Kenya
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Stablecoins, Digital Dollarization, and Financial Self-determination in Kenya
detail.abstract: Kenya has quietly become East Africa's largest stablecoin market, with USD-pegged tokens, overwhelmingly USDT and USDC, now carrying billions of dollars in remittances, crossborder trade settlement, and savings that the country's mobile-money rails handle poorly. This paper argues that the architecture Kenyans have defaulted to is neither neutral nor costless: it imposes a dual-layered sovereignty deficit. At the macro scale, the substitution of foreign digital dollars for the shilling ("digital dollarization") erodes the Central Bank of Kenya's monetary transmission, fractures the country's position under the Impossible Trinity, and channels seigniorage to the United States Treasury through the Treasury-bill reserves backing these tokens. At the micro scale, the same instruments expose individual users to extraterritorial surveillance and unilateral, contract-level asset freezes against which they hold no jurisdictional recourse. The paper's central claim is that these are two distinct problems demanding two distinct architectural responses, and that solving either alone leaves the system compromised. Reclaiming monetary sovereignty requires scaling local-currency stablecoins (such as cKES on the Mento protocol) and anchoring continental settlement on-chain via PAPSS; reclaiming individual sovereignty requires zero-knowledge cryptography, ZK-KYC, and decentralized issuance models that remove corporate freezeswitches. True financial self-determination, the paper contends, demands their integration, a local-currency stablecoin issued natively on a privacy-preserving, decentralized ledger. Using Kenya's Virtual Asset Service Providers Act 2025 as the regulatory anchor, the paper maps the institutional roles, legislative amendments, and user-incentive problems such a stack would confront, and argues that stablecoins should be understood not as consumer products but as instruments of digital statecraft. Though framed around Kenya, the dualsovereignty trilemma it identifies generalizes across emerging Sub-Saharan markets.

detail.title: Leaning Against Inflation Experiences

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
A large share of secular variation in real interest rates can be understood as the effect of monetary policy leaning against experience-based long-run inflation expectations. Survey microdata show that adaptive learning from experienced inflation generates highly persistent, slow-moving long-run inflation expectations. When expectations are shaped by experience, central banks cannot anchor them through communication. Instead, when expectations deviate from the inflation target, monetary policy must remain persistently hawkish or dovish to generate realized inflation outcomes that, through agents’ belief updating, gradually pull long-run expectations back toward the target. Consistent with this mechanism, I find a strong positive relationship between experience-based long-run inflation expectations and real interest rates in the U.S., Germany, the U.K., and Japan. Under their subjective expectations, private-sector agents do not anticipate future reversals in inflation and short-term real interest rates. As a result, long-term real interest rates move with experience-based long-run inflation expectations about as much as short-term real interest rates do, consistent with the data. Secular movements in real rates are also accompanied by persistent patterns in interest-rate forecast errors. Overall, the interaction of monetary policy and learning from experience generates a distinct source of secular real-rate variation, beyond movements in the natural rate of interest.

CV established that CD incorporation transforms irreversible to quasi-reversible redox behaviour across all metal systems, with metal-binding affinity following the trend Fe > Cu ≈ Ni > Zn.

To elucidate the photoluminescence mechanism, DFT calculations at the B3LYP-D3BJ/def2-TZVP level were performed on CA–U assemblies of varying stoichiometry (1:1 to 1:4). The 1:4 CA–U complex was identified as the thermodynamically optimal ratio, forming compact hydrogen-bonded pre-nucleation assemblies (rate-determining barrier: +16.9 kcal/mol) that facilitate sequential dehydration, amide condensation, and intramolecular cyclisation to yield two discrete molecular fluorophores: citrazinic acid (blue emission) and the bicyclic HPPT scaffold (green emission). These predictions were validated by advanced 2D NMR spectroscopy (COSY, HSQC, HMBC, ¹H–¹⁵N HMBC) in DMSO-d₆, which unambiguously confirmed the HPPT structure through characteristic signals at δ ~5.4 ppm and HMBC correlations to imide carbonyl carbons (δC 163–172 ppm).

The surface functionalities identified computationally were exploited in the CD-catalysed three-component synthesis of 2-amino-4H-chromene-3-carbonitrile derivatives from benzaldehyde, malononitrile, and phenolic substrates. The reaction proceeds through a cooperative Knoevenagel condensation–Michael addition–cyclisation–tautomerisation cascade, with CD surface groups acting as bifunctional hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor catalysts. Optimised conditions (ethanol, 60 °C, 10 mg catalyst) afforded isolated yields up to 93% within 2 hours. Two chromene analogues — 2-amino-4-(3-nitrophenyl)- and 2-amino-4-(3-fluoro-4-hydroxyphenyl)-4H-chromene-3-carbonitrile — were synthesised and fully characterised by ¹H NMR.

This work delivers: (i) a green microwave platform for N-CQDs from biogenic precursors; (ii) a DFT-validated, NMR-confirmed molecular description of dual-emissive fluorophore formation with 1:4 CA–U stoichiometry as the critical synthetic parameter; (iii) a CV-based framework for CD–metal interactions; and (iv) a metal-free, heterogeneous CD-catalysed MCR for pharmacologically relevant chromene scaffolds under mild, sustainable conditions. A direct mechanistic analogy between CD fluorophore formation and the chromene catalytic cascade establishes a unified structure–property–function relationship for CA–U-derived carbon dots.

We ask how far the choice of which moments to match can push estimates in misspecified structural models. The answer is: very far. Under regularity conditions, an adversarial researcher informed about the data distribution can choose moments that render any parameter value the unique solution to the population moment-matching problem. Moreover, in many cases they can do so with little increase in model-implied standard errors relative to maximum likelihood. We illustrate both results in a menu-cost model.

detail.title: Perceived Inflation as a State-Dependent Propagation Mechanism in a Behavioral DSGE Model
detail.abstract: This paper studies how consumer perception of inflation emerges from a cognitive process shaped by salience and diagnostic expectations, and how it influences macroeconomic dynamics and monetary policy transmission. Micro evidence shows that exposure to salient price categories generates a persistent and selective perception gap. Embedding this mechanism in a New Keynesian DSGE model in which household decisions and firm pricing respond to perceived inflation yields a perception-based propagation channel. The model is estimated using Simulated Method of Moments and quantitatively matches key features of post-2020 inflation dynamics in Poland. The perception channel amplifies the peak inflation response to a two-standard-deviation energy supply shock by 35 to 45 percent and accounts for a substantial share of post-2020 inflation persistence. The effects are state-dependent, becoming quantitatively important only during large salient shocks. Conditional on the estimated transmission mechanism, optimal policy features a stronger response to inflation, complemented by communication strategies targeting salient consumption categories.

This article examines the implementation of international standards for the prevention and fight against trafficking in children, child abduction, and sexual exploitation within the national legal system of Ukraine. The paper analyzes the normative and legal framework for counteracting child trafficking and kidnapping in Ukraine, with particular attention to Ukraine’s international obligations and the ways in which international legal norms are incorporated into domestic law.

The article discusses the concept of implementation as the actual fulfillment of international obligations at the domestic level, as well as the incorporation of international legal norms into the national legal system. It reviews key stages in the development of Ukraine’s state policy in the field of combating child trafficking and child abduction, including the ratification of international conventions and protocols, criminalization of trafficking in persons, and adoption of national legislation on combating human trafficking.

The study also addresses the legal and practical challenges related to child trafficking, sexual exploitation, victim identification, rehabilitation, institutional support, and the need for improved professional training of specialists working with child victims. The article concludes that Ukraine has joined a wide range of international instruments regulating the prevention of child trafficking, abduction, child prostitution, and child pornography, but further improvement of national legislation, enforcement mechanisms, victim assistance, and public awareness remains necessary.

detail.abstract: This report documents a single narrow event: a user fed Google AI Mode the GallantryAI Living Lexicon and issued an atomic command ("bleach this"). The model did not mirror the document. It extracted the governance logic from within the document and applied it inward to its own output register — then explained its own mechanism in the researcher's language. A search of existing literature found no recorded instances of this specific pattern. Researchers name adjacent phenomena — Self-Refine, Self-Calibration, adversarial prompting — but none document user-authored governance being turned inward by the model from a document mid-session. The same session produced independent technical validation of GallantryAI's core mechanics and a new cross-model linguistic finding: the researcher's own phrase inventory appearing at structurally significant moments across different architectures. This is named here as the Inverse Uglyography Finding.

detail.abstract: Using Chinese manufacturing and customs data, we study capital upgrading through capital-substitution episodes, in which firms invest in capital while reducing employment. These episodes are followed by higher productivity, wages, and skill intensity, and, importantly, are accompanied by capital-goods-specific import adjustment consistent with upgrading. A WTO-induced demand boom reduces capital-substitution frequency and reallocates continuing capital-goods spending toward lower-price products. detail.abstract: In a model with endogenous risk-taking, deposit insurance and limited liability may lead banks to make risky loans that are socially inefficient. detail.abstract: Peripheral urban communities in Lagos face persistent challenges of infrastructure provision, limited public services, weak institutional representation, and uneven state presence. Yet these communities are not governance vacuums. Across peripheral territories, civic-community organisations coordinate collective action, facilitate participation, mediate community-state relations, and organise local responses to governance challenges. Drawing on participatory action research conducted between June 2021 and February 2026 across four peripheral communities in Lagos (Makoko, Ajegunle, Mushin, and Agege), this paper examines how community-based organisations operate as non-formal governance actors through five interconnected functions: participation mediation, local coordination, informal governance, civic mobilisation, and social support. The theoretical framework draws on hybrid governance theory (Kooiman, 2003; Meagher et al., 2014), Milton Santos's theory of territory and peripheral urban space (1996, 2000), Paulo Freire's popular education framework (1970), and Ostrom's collective action theory (1990). Fieldwork evidence shows that these organisations increasingly perform governance functions that shape collective decision-making and local coordination where formal institutions are inconsistently present. Their growing importance raises important questions about representation, accountability, and the risk of normalising long-term state withdrawal. The paper contributes to debates on hybrid governance, urban informality, popular education, territorial development, and community participation in the Global South.

title: Moral Design of Algorithmic Governance

detail.title: Moral Design of Algorithmic Governance
detail.abstract: When governments deploy algorithmic enforcement systems, they do not merely automate policy; they encode distributive choices about who bears the cost of institutional error. Every such system embeds an error-allocation specification: a loss function fixing the relative cost of false positives and false negatives in training and a decision threshold crystallizing those costs at deployment. This article classifies that specification as a legislative rule under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and its state analogues, such that adopting it through default procurement is unlawful subdelegation that bypasses notice and comment where the duty attaches. Behaviorally, these configurations persist as a choice-architecture problem: the default effect that drives organ-donation and retirement-savings behavior also operates, selectively, on the engineers who configure public-sector systems, entrenching configurations congenial to institutional incentives. It maps the second Mathews v. Eldridge factor onto error-cost allocation and pairs Mechanism Design with a democratic "Moral Design" framework and test. The argument yields five remedies ordered as a penalty-default architecture: error-allocation disclosure tied to procurement; legislative error budgets; Algorithmic Impact Statements with public comment; periodic democratic review; and a bifurcated Blackstone evidentiary presumption that reads the implied error-cost ratio off the disclosed configuration, administered by an Algorithmic Choice Architecture Review Board.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces and formally defines the Atomic Language Control Model (ALCM): a framework mapping individual natural-language words to specific, enumerated output dimensions in AI reasoning-not as style or tone, but as mechanical axis positions. The paper documents eight primary axes and a ninth spatial axis, traces the framework's origin in field observation across six AI platforms, grounds it in existing research on modal verb effects, pragmatic framing, and linguistic prompt sensitivity, names multi-axis collision as the primary mechanism behind short prompt power, and argues that word-level axis awareness is one of the most foundational skills in practical prompt governance.
