detail.title: The Business-Fluent Lawyer: Key Concepts in Technology, Governance, Ethics, and Behavioral Science for Legal Practice
detail.abstract: Modern legal professionals face complex client challenges that arrive as business and technological crises with heavy legal dimensions. Many practitioners, however, lack the crossdisciplinary fluency needed to navigate these frameworks. This paper addresses that gap by examining essential contemporary concepts across corporate governance, employment law, emerging technology, cognitive psychology, and professional ethics. The analysis makes four substantive contributions. First, it demonstrates that cognitive biases represent internal professional risks that doctrinal expertise alone cannot neutralize, making self-awareness a professional obligation. Second, it distinguishes between the legal risk profiles of generative AI and large language models, showing that conflating them leads to misidentification of applicable legal frameworks. Third, it reframes DEI and discrimination as a unified topic requiring engagement with the full spectrum of bias. Finally, it surveys emerging technologies such as emotion AI, quantum computing, and blockchain, for which regulatory frameworks are still being developed. The paper concludes that technical competence is no longer sufficient on its own. Modern clients require trusted advisors who can ensure responsible, trustworthy conduct. This cross-disciplinary vocabulary is the working language of sophisticated modern practice.

detail.abstract: Salespeople play a critical role in determining the success of sales organizations through their performance. However, existing research has predominantly focused on Western contexts, with limited attention to highly spiritual markets where religiosity significantly influences personal and professional life. This study aims to examine the factors affecting salespeople’s performance within such a context. Adopting a qualitative approach, this study utilizes thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with 24 high-performing life insurance salespeople in Indonesia. The findings identify four key categories influencing sales performance: salesperson, organization, buyer, and competitor. Among these, the salesperson category emerges as the most dominant. Notably, spirituality and family support are identified as two important and previously underexplored factors within this category. These findings contribute to the literature by reinforcing the central role of individual-level factors in driving sales performance while extending the discussion to include spiritual and familial dimensions. The results suggest that sales organizations should not only focus on developing selling skills and providing organizational support but also consider the internal values and personal well-being of salespeople. Encouraging alignment between work, personal beliefs, and family support may enhance sustainable sales performance, particularly in highly spiritual markets.

title: The AI Trap: How Over-Reliance On Generative AI Undermines Professional Development For Law Students And Young Attorneys
affiliations: Nova Southeastern University Shepard Broad College of Law

detail.title: The AI Trap: How Over-Reliance On Generative AI Undermines Professional Development For Law Students And Young Attorneys
detail.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence tools can produce legal memoranda, draft contracts, conduct legal research, and edit drafts with remarkable efficiency. For an overwhelmed law student staring at a blank page or a first-year associate racing against a billing deadline, these capabilities are enormously seductive. However, there is a hidden cost to this seduction that the legal profession has yet to fully address. While AI can enable law students and young attorneys to produce work product that appears competent, the use of AI alone does not develop the underlying analytical skills to assess or reproduce AI’s output. This Article argues that over-reliance on AI during the formative developmental period creates a dangerous gap between apparent and actual competence, a condition this Article calls the Competence Illusion.

Drawing on cognitive science research on skill acquisition, legal writing pedagogy, professional ethics, and empirical studies of AI's impact on legal tasks, this Article examines the mechanisms by which AI over-reliance produces borrowed competence in place of genuine expertise and provides targeted guidance for the three audiences most at risk: law students, young attorneys, and supervising attorneys responsible for their development.

The argument is not that AI is inherently harmful. However, AI shortcuts that replace intellectual exertion, struggle, feedback, and revision undermine lasting competence. Thus, while lawyers may use AI proficiently, those who are methodologically ill-equipped may lack critical professional development, meaning that they will be unable to practice law competently without AI. When those high-stakes moments arrive, including the bar examination, the courtroom, and the client emergency, the Competence Illusion fails, and the consequences fall on the lawyer.

Law school provides valuable training in legal analysis, research, and writing, but it often gives students only limited exposure to important aspects of legal practice.  This article offers practical advice to law students about how to make the most of their legal education and prepare themselves for effective practice.

The article identifies ten things that law students can do to develop knowledge, skills, relationships, and professional judgment that may not receive sufficient attention in traditional law school courses.  These include understanding the realities of legal practice, taking responsibility for one's own education, developing an ethical and satisfying professional identity, communicating effectively, thinking strategically about cases and clients, focusing on client decision-making, learning to represent clients in mediation, using artificial intelligence responsibly, and maintaining personal well-being. The article emphasizes that students should not assume that merely completing the formal curriculum automatically prepares them for practice.  By actively shaping their own education and seeking experiences beyond the classroom, students can enter practice with greater confidence, competence, and satisfaction.

detail.abstract:
This illustrated guide provides a brief, practical introduction to the appropriate use of AI in dispute resolution.  It encourages parties to use AI to help them think more clearly rather than to rely on AI to predict outcomes or make decisions.  The guide explains common mistakes people make when using AI, discusses confidentiality and privacy risks, and offers practical suggestions for evaluating AI-generated information.

The guide uses plain language, visual design, and principles of universal design to make these ideas accessible to broad audiences, including self-represented parties and people with varying levels of legal knowledge and literacy.  The illustrations are intended to communicate key ideas quickly and reinforce good decision-making practices.

The guide is a resource that courts, dispute resolution programs, lawyers, mediators, and educators can use to help parties use AI appropriately.  The guide may also serve as a teaching resource in legal and dispute resolution education, helping students, trainees, and practitioners learn how to use AI appropriately and how to help clients and parties use AI effectively.  A companion text guide, Using AI in Mediation: A Guide for Parties, provides more detailed guidance for parties participating in mediation.

In addition to its practical purpose, the guide illustrates an approach to legal and dispute resolution education that combines good decision-making principles, plain language, universal design, and visual communication.  As self-represented parties increasingly use AI in disputes, courts and dispute resolution programs are likely to need educational resources like this to help parties use AI appropriately.

detail.title: Extracted PhD Thesis on Impact of Adoption of Electronic Human Resource Management on Performance of Employees in Bangladesh
detail.abstract:
Performance of employees is the lifeline of every organization a firm that aims to put maximum effort into obtaining the desired outcome. Therefore, the unitary role of human resources management becomes more extensive and versatile. The demands of the new century pose a new challenge to people management functions, requiring them to adopt new ways of work and bid farewell to classical methods. The new way of working is heavily reliant on technology. It replaced man with machines and pen with keyboards.

The major attempt of the study is to assess the role of adopting electronic human resource management on performance of employees in Bangladesh. While investigating the association, the study also measured the role of knowledge-sharing behavior and top management support. In accordance to an extensive literature review, the research developed a four-dimensional model of electronic human resource management, encompassing eRecruitment and selection, eTraining and development, ePerformance appraisal, and eCompensation and payroll, as well as unidimensional model of performance of employees, knowledge sharing behavior, and top management support. The model of the study has been drawn under the lens of technology accepted model and social exchange theory. This quantitative research collected data from 320 respondents with the help of structured questionnaire and analyzed data. After finishing the pretesting, the study conducted a pilot survey. The survey, as indicated by the final questionnaire, began after confirmation of validity and reliability. By applying a seven -point Likert scale, the data coded and analyzed using statistical software such as SPSS and SmartPLS version 4. Specifically, the software applied in descriptive analysis, reliability testing, common method bias tests, factor loading, structural equation modeling, model fit tests, and other applications.

The research attempted an emerging issue and produced exciting findings. The adoption of ePerformance appraisal does not significantly influence performance of employees. In contrast, eRcruitment and selection, eTraining and development, and eCompensation and payrolls have a significant impact on performance of employees. Similarly, the knowledgesharing behavior mediates (fully or partially) the association between four-dimensional electronic human resource adoption and performance of employees except the nexus between electronic recruitment and selection to performance of employees. On the other hand, top management support does not moderate the association between knowledge  sharing behavior and performance of employees. Moreover, the open-ended questionnaire provided meaningful insights, including performance of employee’s comparisons before and after the adoption of electronic human resource management, positive consequences, challenges encountered, a list of available software, and employee suggestions for efficient adoption.

The outcome of this emerging research will significantly contribute to organizations in reassessing their existing adoption levels and guiding firms that are planning for future adoption. Keeping performance of employees as a priority, the firm may introduce technology-based workplaces, implement necessary policies for knowledge sharing, and encourage greater involvement from top management to enable employees to perform at their best. Practitioners may apply the outcome to handle the performance management and technology adoption matters. The research experience suggested that future research may be conducted with a bigger sample size, employ different tools and techniques, and include comparative analysis between the government and private sectors, as well as case study-based research, in the context of Bangladesh.

title: Prediction, Not Adjudication: Why Crowdsourced Blockchain Decisions Are Not Arbitral Awards
affiliations: University of Oxford - Faculty of Law and University of Oxford - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Prediction, Not Adjudication: Why Crowdsourced Blockchain Decisions Are Not Arbitral Awards
detail.abstract: In this article, we argue that decisions produced by crowdsourced blockchain dispute-resolution systems such as Kleros and Polymarket's UMA protocol do not qualify as arbitral awards. Their defining feature is that they reward participants for predicting what the majority of other participants will decide. Arbitration, by contrast, is oriented towards finding the right answer through independent judgment, deliberation, and reasoned decision-making. Guessing may sometimes produce the correct result, but it is categorically different from adjudication. The fact that a crowd occasionally reaches the right answer does not transform a process of prediction into a process of judgment.

title: Beyond AI Adoption: How Curiosity and Reflection Shape Innovative Behavior in Technology-Enabled Workplaces

detail.title: Beyond AI Adoption: How Curiosity and Reflection Shape Innovative Behavior in Technology-Enabled Workplaces
detail.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming contemporary workplaces, yet employees vary considerably in their ability to convert AI use into innovative outcomes. Addressing this gap, this study examines the psychological mechanism and boundary condition underlying the relationship between GenAI use and employee innovative behavior. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework and information-gap theory, we propose that work-related curiosity mediates the effect of GenAI use on innovation, while individual reflection strengthens this process. The proposed moderated mediation model was tested using multi-source supervisor–employee dyadic data from 315 employees and 72 supervisors working in project-based technology firms in an emerging economy. Covariance-based structural equation modeling and bootstrapping analyses revealed that GenAI use positively predicts both work-related curiosity and innovative behavior. Work-related curiosity partially mediates the relationship between GenAI use and innovation, indicating that GenAI stimulates innovation by fostering employees’ intrinsic motivation to explore, learn, and experiment. Furthermore, individual reflection positively moderates the effect of GenAI use on curiosity, such that the indirect effect of GenAI on innovative behavior is significantly stronger among highly reflective employees. By identifying curiosity as a critical motivational mechanism and reflection as an important dispositional boundary condition, this study advances understanding of how and when GenAI contributes to employee innovation. The findings extend AI-at-work research beyond instrumental explanations of technology use and provide evidence from an underexamined emerging-economy context. Practically, organizations can enhance innovation outcomes by promoting curiosity-oriented GenAI use and embedding reflective work practices.

detail.abstract: Researchers are faced with the choice of which of the many recently developed difference-in-differences methods to use in practice. To assess these estimators' relative performance for single-unit event studies, we conduct 134,000+ state-level placebo event studies across 13 estimators. We find that no single method dominates. Performance is context-dependent, with synthetic-control-like methods sometimes outperforming and sometimes underperforming two-way-fixed-effect-like and matching methods. Performance also varies across states at least as much as it does across estimators. Our results highlight the need for practitioners to conduct placebo tests to understand the performance of methods in their research context.

detail.abstract: The sequence-space Jacobian (SSJ) method of Auclert et al. (2021a) has made heterogeneous-agent models far easier to solve, fueling an explosion of applications. But even SSJ strains against capacity constraints when state spaces grow very large, as in economies with overlapping generations of heterogeneous agents (HA-OLG). We show how to exploit the special properties of age—finite planning horizons and deterministic transitions between ages—to compute the Jacobians of a general class of HA-OLG models orders of magnitude faster. We provide rigorous proofs, age-specific Jacobians that decompose aggregate dynamics across cohorts, an application to the dynamic general-equilibrium effects of secularly declining birth rates, and an accessible cookbook for adopting our method.

title: Stop Debugging the Dreamer: A Manager’s Framework for Turning AI Hallucinations into Breakthroughs

detail.title: Stop Debugging the Dreamer: A Manager’s Framework for Turning AI Hallucinations into Breakthroughs
detail.abstract: Most organizations treat generative AI’s hallucinations as a defect to stamp out. That instinct is backwards. Discovery has always run on the same engine — abundant variation, then ruthless selection — and generative AI has made variation almost free. The binding constraint is no longer imagination but verification, and verification cost is something managers can deliberately lower. We give managers a diagnostic, the Verifiability–Stakes matrix, that says when to amplify a model’s “dreaming,” when to harness it behind a verification gate, and when to contain it. More importantly, we show a dynamic move competitors miss: by engineering verification cheaper, a firm can tip whole domains from “too risky to touch” into “too valuable to ignore.” A four-step protocol — Provoke, Filter, Capture, Bound — builds the organization that turns AI’s errors into advantage — and tells you fast, before the expensive bet, when it is not paying.

detail.title: Disruptive vs. Collaborative Positioning and the Cost of Talent: Evidence from Startup Hiring Field Experiments

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Business School Research Paper Forthcoming

detail.abstract: We examine how a startup's strategic positioning, including whether it frames its technology and market approach as disruptive or collaborative, affects talent acquisition in new ventures. Although prior research has examined how disruptive positioning influences investors, its impact on prospective employees remains less well understood. We conduct two preregistered field experiments with an early-stage climate-technology startup in India, randomly assigning prospective software engineers to receive disruptive, collaborative, or, in the second experiment, neutral positioning language while holding all other job and firm attributes constant. Across both experiments, positioning affected candidates' perceptions of the opportunity. In Field Experiment 1, when candidates encountered positioning early in the application process, disruptive positioning reduced application completion by 6 percentage points and, conditional on completion, increased compensation demands by nearly 5% relative to collaborative positioning. In Field Experiment 2, where treatment was introduced later, completion rates did not differ significantly, yet candidates exposed to disruptive positioning demanded 9% higher total compensation than those exposed to collaborative positioning. Benchmarking against a neutral control suggests that this gap was driven primarily by collaborative positioning lowering compensation demands relative to baseline expectations. Follow-up evidence from interviews and a survey experiment suggests that disruptive positioning increased perceptions of technological novelty, specialized skill requirements, and effort demands. Consistent with this mechanism, the compensation gap was concentrated among more experienced and higher-earning candidates. Overall, our findings demonstrate that strategic positioning affects candidates' willingness to engage with startup employment, impacting the cost of attracting talent.

title: CROSS-SELLING GOVERNANCE

detail.title: CROSS-SELLING GOVERNANCE
detail.abstract: Corporate governance faces threats from all sides-not just the familiar narratives of CEO malfeasance and inattentive directors, but lawyers, bankers, accountants, management consultants, and other professional service providers (PSPs) who engage in cross-selling. Cross-selling, or leveraging an existing client relationship to sell additional services, is a ubiquitous business strategy. While it may create opportunities for corporate clients, it can also lead to abuses. The quality of PSP advice, upon which company directors and officers often rely to fulfill their fiduciary duties and responsibilities, can be undermined. Existing regulation of PSP cross-selling does not adequately address corporate governance risks. Their elimination will require a synthesis of both regulatory and private ordering approaches.

title: Predicting Employee Attrition Using Machine Learning: A Comparative Analysis of Classification Models for Human Resource Analytics

detail.title: Predicting Employee Attrition Using Machine Learning: A Comparative Analysis of Classification Models for Human Resource Analytics
detail.abstract: Employee attrition-the voluntary resignation of employees from an organization-represents one of the most significant challenges facing human resource management today. The cost of replacing a single employee can reach up to 200% of their annual salary, making accurate attrition prediction a strategic priority for organizations worldwide. This study presents a comparative analysis of three machine learning models-Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost-for predicting employee attrition using the IBM HR Analytics Employee Attrition dataset comprising 1,470 employee records and 31 features. Each model was evaluated across five performance metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and ROC-AUC. Results demonstrate that Logistic Regression achieved the highest predictive performance with an accuracy of 87.41% and ROC-AUC of 0.8057, outperforming Random Forest (ROC-AUC: 0.7890) and XGBoost (ROC-AUC: 0.7580). Feature importance analysis identified total working years, overtime, and stock option level as the strongest predictors of attrition. These findings provide empirical evidence for model selection in enterprise HR analytics systems and offer actionable insights for workforce retention strategy design.

title: Stories People Hear About Inflation

detail.title: Stories People Hear About Inflation
detail.abstract: Households form inflation expectations not only from observed price changes and official statistics, but also from the stories they hear about inflation. Using more than 350,000 podcast episodes, I study how inflation is discussed in public media. I distinguish between causal stories, which link inflation to mechanisms such as housing shortages, oil shocks, sanctions, or monetary policy, and stories which assign responsibility to political actors or institutions without a clear causal account. To estimate their effects, I exploit recurring podcast guests who repeat similar explanations across shows reaching different local audiences. Stories centered on war, oil shocks, sanctions, and trade conflict lower short term inflation expectations, though the effect fades at longer horizons. Partisan blame stories are associated with higher expectations, but the evidence points to audience selection rather than persuasion. Overall, the paper shows that public stories about inflation matter: some move expectations by changing how households interpret economic shocks, while others reveal the political sorting of media audiences.

detail.abstract: This article explores how the context for crafting trade policy is changing, particularly when considering the digitalisation of trade, and what it could imply for the role of NTFCs in fostering modernisation. Mainstreaming digital technologies in trade facilitation reform is not merely an obligation for most countries, it is a necessity. Indeed, conditions for the cost-effective and rapid movement of goods can have as much to do with a product's data as with a product itself. This is increasingly the case as the shift toward paperless trade is premised on policy delivery and compliance through digital means. Yet, disparate and emergent rules/regulations (e.g. General Data Protection Regulation, European data strategy), arrangements (e.g. Digital Economy Partnership Agreement), framework treaties (e.g. Cross-border Paperless Trade in Asia and the Pacific), and provisions (e.g. e-commerce chapters in trade agreements) highlight a need to coordinate all relevant legal and technical communities when crafting 'future proof' policies at the national level. In addition, modern supply chain models specify relationships between data entities in international sales/transport contracts and demand a reformulation of measures in accordance with the broadening scope of channels (e.g. cross-border e-commerce) and modes of policy delivery (e.g. the Internet).

title: Distillation and Strategic Launches on the LLM Frontier: An Empirical Analysis
affiliations: University at Buffalo (SUNY) - School of Management and University at Buffalo (SUNY) - School of Management

detail.title: Distillation and Strategic Launches on the LLM Frontier: An Empirical Analysis
detail.abstract: We study how distillation shapes the innovation frontier in the large language model (LLM) market. A distinctive feature of this market is that launches can also become inputs into rivals’ subsequent development: Model behavior can be learned from, and open-weight releases expose reusable artifacts more directly. We build a provider-week panel from 529 model launches by 51 providers between November 2022 and June 2026, measuring both launch decisions and benchmark-based quality states. Reduced-form evidence identifies two opposing margins: While realized open-weight rival frontier raises in the same capability dimension are associated with larger subsequent quality improvements, anticipated near-term open-weight rival launches reduce current launch probabilities. Closed-weight rival activity does not exhibit similar patterns. We then estimate a structural launch model in which distillation affects both quality improvement and launch timing. Counterfactual analyses show that an all-closed-weight regime increases launch frequency but reduces quality gains per launch, whereas an all-open-weight regime tempers launch frequency but increases quality gains per launch. These opposing margins offset more strongly under all-open than under all-closed: All-open remains close to the baseline frontier, while all-closed yields greater total quality improvement through a substantially higher launch frequency. Impacts on consumers are modest and dimension-specific, with the all-open regime tending to benefit consumers more than the all-closed regime by improving the best available models. Our work highlights how distillation and model openness reshape the LLM innovation frontier through timing and magnitude.

detail.title: Examining the Impact of Brexit and COVID-19 Pandemic on Sovereign and Bank Systemic Risk Co-Movements: A Value-at-Risk and Wavelet Analysis
detail.abstract: : We analyze the impact on financial markets of two major, overlapping sources of uncertainty, the UK exit from the European Union and the pandemic. We examine how these compounded events have impacted the co-movement between systemic sovereign risk and systemic bank risk, utilizing Value-at-Risk (VaR) and wavelet-based methodologies. Systemic risk is measured in terms of sovereign and bank credit default swap (CDS) spreads for the United Kingdom, as well as for selected countries. In our analysis, wavelets capture the dynamic interdependencies and lead-lag relationships between sovereign and banking risk time series. For robustness, we use sovereign bond spreads as an alternative proxy for systemic risk. We found strong temporal correlations in systemic bank risk with a sovereign-driven pattern characterizing the EU and the USA during the pandemic. Moreover, we show that the co-movements between sovereign and bank systemic risks and broader financial systemic risk feature the influence of market dynamics on sovereign and banking activities.

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: Within narrowly defined industries, the most productive firms produce far more than the least productive from the same inputs, and this dispersion widens in downturns. We build a tractable representative-agent model in which financial frictions—adverse selection and moral hazard—make firms sort endogenously into lenders, strategic defaulters, and producers. As credit conditions vary, the resulting misallocation gives aggregate total factor productivity (TFP) an endogenous component that accounts for about 30 percent of the variance of TFP at business-cycle frequencies, a third of it from strategic default. We show that our tractable model can match key features of the observed distribution of productivity across firms and its co-movement with output growth and credit conditions in the data.
